refs.quote: BYSTOLIC is indicated for the treatment of hypertension, to lower blood pressure

For most patients, the recommended starting dose is 5 mg once daily, with or without food, as monotherapy or in combination with other agents. For patients requiring further reduction in blood pressure, the dose can be increased at 2-week intervals up to 40 mg.

Nebivolol is a β-adrenergic receptor blocking agent. In extensive metabolizers (most of the population) and at doses less than or equal to 10 mg, nebivolol is preferentially β 1 selective. In poor metabolizers and at higher doses, nebivolol inhibits both β 1 - and β 2 - adrenergic receptors.

mg_safety.note: Beta-adrenergic blockers carry class caution in myasthenia gravis; no specific MG warning appears in the nebivolol label.

pgx.value: Metabolized via CYP2D6 hydroxylation. CYP2D6 poor metabolizers (PMs) attain 5-fold higher Cmax and 10-fold higher AUC of d-nebivolol (half-life 19 h vs 12 h in extensive metabolizers) and lose beta1-selectivity. However, no dose adjustments are necessary for CYP2D6 PMs because active hydroxyl and glucuronide metabolites contribute to beta-blocking activity.

refs.quote: No dose adjustments are necessary for patients who are CYP2D6 poor metabolizers. The clinical effect and safety profile observed in poor metabolizers were similar to those of extensive metabolizers
For the same dose, PMs attain a 5-fold higher Cmax and 10-fold higher AUC of d-nebivolol than do EMs.
somnolence, syncope, thrombocytopenia, various rashes and skin disorders, vertigo, and vomiting.

mechanism_of_action.value: Beta-adrenergic receptor blocking agent (preferentially beta1-selective at <=10 mg in extensive metabolizers; inhibits both beta1 and beta2 receptors in poor metabolizers and at higher doses), lacking intrinsic sympathomimetic and membrane-stabilizing activity. Possible antihypertensive mechanisms include decreased heart rate, decreased myocardial contractility, diminution of tonic sympathetic outflow, suppression of renin activity, and vasodilation.

refs.quote: Possible factors that may be involved include: (1) decreased heart rate, (2) decreased myocardial contractility, (3) diminution of tonic sympathetic outflow to the periphery from cerebral vasomotor centers, (4) suppression of renin activity and (5) vasodilation and decreased peripheral vascular resistance.
Nebivolol is predominantly metabolized via direct glucuronidation of parent and to a lesser extent via N-dealkylation and oxidation via cytochrome P450 2D6.

value.effect: CYP2D6 inhibition increases nebivolol plasma levels (fluoxetine increased d-nebivolol AUC 8-fold and Cmax 3-fold).
value.management: Use caution; monitor patients closely and adjust nebivolol dose according to blood pressure response.

refs.quote: Use caution when BYSTOLIC is co-administered with CYP2D6 inhibitors (quinidine, propafenone, fluoxetine, paroxetine, etc.)

Fluoxetine, a CYP2D6 inhibitor, administered at 20 mg per day for 21 days prior to a single 10 mg dose of nebivolol to 10 healthy adults, led to an 8-fold increase in the AUC and 3-fold increase in C max for d-nebivolol

value.management: Do not use BYSTOLIC with other beta-blockers.

refs.quote: Do not use BYSTOLIC with other β-blockers.

value.effect: Excessive reduction of sympathetic activity; rebound hypertension risk with clonidine withdrawal.
value.management: Closely monitor patients receiving catecholamine-depleting drugs. In patients receiving BYSTOLIC and clonidine, discontinue BYSTOLIC for several days before gradual tapering of clonidine.

refs.quote: Closely monitor patients receiving catecholamine-depleting drugs, such as reserpine or guanethidine, because the added β-blocking action of BYSTOLIC may produce excessive reduction of sympathetic activity. In patients who are receiving BYSTOLIC and clonidine, discontinue BYSTOLIC for several days before the gradual tapering of clonidine.

value.effect: Both digitalis glycosides and beta-blockers slow AV conduction and decrease heart rate, increasing risk of bradycardia.
value.management: Monitor heart rate and AV conduction.

refs.quote: Both digitalis glycosides and β-blockers slow atrioventricular conduction and decrease heart rate. Concomitant use can increase the risk of bradycardia.

value.drug_or_class: Calcium Channel Blockers (verapamil, diltiazem) and Antiarrhythmics (disopyramide)
value.effect: Exacerbates myocardial depression and AV conduction inhibition, causing excessive reductions in heart rate, blood pressure, and cardiac contractility.
value.management: Monitor heart rate, blood pressure, and cardiac function closely when co-administering.

refs.quote: BYSTOLIC can exacerbate the effects of myocardial depressants or inhibitors of AV conduction, such as certain calcium antagonists (particularly of the phenylalkylamine [verapamil] and benzothiazepine [diltiazem] classes), or antiarrhythmic agents, such as disopyramide.
CYP2D6 enzyme inhibitors may increase nebivolol levels. ( 7.1 ) Reserpine or clonidine may produce excessive reduction of sympathetic activity. ( 7.2 )

tier.note: 5-axis synthesis: (1) No Boxed Warning or pregnancy contraindication. (2) Human data insufficient to determine drug-associated developmental risks; third-trimester beta-blocker exposure increases neonatal risk of hypotension, bradycardia, hypoglycemia, and respiratory depression. (3) Rat studies showed embryofetal/perinatal lethality at ~1.2x MRHD (40 mg/day), though rabbit studies up to 10x MRHD were negative. (4) Uncontrolled maternal hypertension increases preeclampsia, IUGR, and intrauterine death risks. (5) PLLR label. Assigned caution.

refs.quote: Available data regarding use of BYSTOLIC in pregnant women are insufficient to determine whether there are drug-associated risks of adverse developmental outcomes. There are risks to the mother and fetus associated with poorly controlled hypertension in pregnancy. The use of beta blockers during the third trimester of pregnancy may increase the risk of hypotension, bradycardia, hypoglycemia

lactation_rid.value: No human breast milk data available

refs.quote: Quantitative human breast milk concentrations of nebivolol are unavailable. Summary of Use during Lactation: Because nebivolol has no human milk data and accumulates more in lipid-rich compartments than labetalol or metoprolol, prefer labetalol or metoprolol during breastfeeding, especially with newborn or preterm infants. There is no information regarding the presence of nebivolol in human milk, the effects on the breastfed infant, or the effects on milk production. Nebivolol is present in rat milk [see Data]. Because of the potential for β-blockers to produce serious adverse reactions in nursing infants, especially bradycardia, BYSTOLIC is not recommended during nursing.
